L97@P1: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes how Swagger specifications are processed by
L98@P1: RESTler. Sections III and IV present the main test-generation
L99@P1: algorithm used in RESTler and implementation details. Section V presents an evaluation of the test-generation techniques
L100@P1: and search strategies implemented in RESTler. Section VI

L102@P1: experiences fuzzing several public cloud services. Section VIII

L104@P1: II. PROCESSING API SPECIFICATIONS
L105@P1: In this paper, we consider services accessible through REST
L106@P1: APIs described with a Swagger specification. A client program
L107@P1: can send messages, called requests, to a service and receive
L108@P1: messages back, called responses. Such messages are sent over
L109@P1: the HTTP protocol. A Swagger specification describes how to
L110@P1: access a service through its REST API (e.g., what requests
L111@P1: the service can handle and what responses may be expected).
L112@P1: Given a Swagger specification, open-source Swagger tools can
L113@P1: automatically generate a web UI that allows users to view the
L114@P1: documentation and interact with the API via a web browser.
L115@P1: A sample Swagger specification, in web-UI form, is shown

L198@P1: III. TEST GENERATION ALGORITHM
L199@P1: The main algorithm for test generation used by RESTler is
L200@P1: shown in Figure 3 in python-like notation. It starts (line 3) by
L201@P1: processing a Swagger specification as discussed in the previous
L202@P1: section. The result of this processing is a set of request types,
L203@P1: denoted reqSet in Figure 3, and of their dependencies (more
L204@P1: on this later).
L205@P1: The algorithm computes a set of request sequences, as inferred from Swagger, denoted seqSet and initially containing
L206@P1: an empty sequence  (line 5). A request sequence is valid if
L207@P1: every response in the sequence has a valid return code, defined
L208@P1: here as any code in the 200 range. At each iteration of its main
L209@P1: loop (line 8), starting with n = 1, the algorithm computes all
L210@P1: valid request sequences seqSet of length n before moving to
L211@P1: n+1 and so on until a user-specified maxLength is reached.
L212@P1: Computing seqSet is done in two steps.
L213@P1: First, the set of valid request sequences of length n − 1 is
L214@P1-2: extended (line 9) to create a set of new sequences of length n1 Inputs: swagger spec, maxLength
L215@P2: 2 # Set of requests parsed from the Swagger API spec
L216@P2: 3 reqSet = PROCESS(swagger spec)
L217@P2: 4 # Set of request sequences (initially an empty sequence )
L218@P2: 5 seqSet = {}
L219@P2: 6 # Main loop: iterate up to a given maximum sequence length
L220@P2: 7 n = 1
L221@P2: 8 while (n =< maxLength):
L222@P2: 9 seqSet = EXTEND(seqSet, reqSet)
L223@P2: 10 seqSet = RENDER(seqSet)
L224@P2: 11 n = n + 1
L225@P2: 12 # Extend all sequences in seqSet by appending
L226@P2: 13 # new requests whose dependencies are satisfied
L227@P2: 14 def EXTEND(seqSet, reqSet):
L228@P2: 15 newSeqSet = {}
L229@P2: 16 for seq in seqSet:
L230@P2: 17 for req in reqSet:
L231@P2: 18 if DEPENDENCIES(seq, req):
L232@P2: 19 newSeqSet = newSeqSet + concat(seq, req)
L233@P2: 20 return newSeqSet
L234@P2: 21 # Concretize all newly appended requests using dictionary values,
L235@P2: 22 # execute each new request sequence and keep the valid ones
L236@P2: 23 def RENDER(seqSet):
L237@P2: 24 newSeqSet = {}
L238@P2: 25 for seq in seqSet:
L239@P2: 26 req = last request in(seq)
L240@P2: 27 V~ = tuple of fuzzable types in(req)
L241@P2: 28 for ~v in V~ :
L242@P2: 29 newReq = concretize(req, ~v)
L243@P2: 30 newSeq = concat(seq, newReq)
L244@P2: 31 response = EXECUTE(newSeq)
L245@P2: 32 if response has a valid code:
L246@P2: 33 newSeqSet = newSeqSet + newSeq
L247@P2: 34 else:
L248@P2: 35 log error
L249@P2: 36 return newSeqSet
L250@P2: 37 # Check that all objects referenced in a request are produced
L251@P2: 38 # by some response in a prior request sequence
L252@P2: 39 def DEPENDENCIES(seq, req):
L253@P2: 40 if CONSUMES(req) ⊆ PRODUCES(seq):
L254@P2: 41 return True
L255@P2: 42 else:
L256@P2: 43 return False
L257@P2: 44 # Objects required in a request
L258@P2: 45 def CONSUMES(req):
L259@P2: 46 return object types required in(req)
L260@P2: 47 # Objects produced in the responses of a sequence of requests
L261@P2: 48 def PRODUCES(seq):
L262@P2: 49 dynamicObjects = {}
L263@P2: 50 for req in seq:
L264@P2: 51 newObjs = objects produced in response of(req)
L265@P2: 52 dynamicObjects = dynamicObjects + newObjs
L266@P2: 53 return dynamicObjects
L267@P2: Fig. 3: Main Algorithm used in RESTler.
L268@P2: by appending each request with satisfied dependencies at the
L269@P2: end of each sequence, as described in the EXTEND function
L270@P2: (line 14). The function DEPENDENCIES (line 39) checks if
L271@P2: all dependencies of the specified request are satisfied. This is
L272@P2: true when every dynamic object that is a required parameter
L273@P2: of the request, denoted by CONSUMES(req), is produced by
L274@P2: some response to the request sequence preceding it, denoted
L275@P2: by PRODUCES(seq). If all the dependencies are satisfied,
L276@P2: the new sequence of length n is retained (line 19); otherwise
L277@P2: it is discarded.
L278@P2: Second, each newly-extended request sequence whose dependencies are satisfied is rendered (line 10) one by one as
L279@P2: described in the RENDER function (line 23). For every newlyappended request (line 26), the list of all fuzzable primitive
L280@P2: types in the request is computed (line 27) (those are identified
L281@P2: by restler_fuzzable in the code shown on the right of
L282@P2: Figure 2). Then, each fuzzable primitive type in the request is
L283@P2: concretized, which substitutes one concrete value of that type
L284@P2: taken out of a finite, user-configurable dictionary of values.
L285@P2: For instance, for fuzzable type integer, RESTler might use
L286@P2: a small dictionary with the values 0, 1, and -10, while for
L287@P2: fuzzable type string, a dictionary could be defined with
L288@P2: the values “sampleString”, the empty string, and a very long
L289@P2: fixed string. The function RENDER generates all possible such
L290@P2: combinations (line 28). Each combination thus corresponds
L291@P2: to a fully-defined request newReq (line 29) which is HTTPsyntactically correct. The function RENDER then executes this
L292@P2: new request sequence (line 31), and checks its response: if the
L293@P2: response has a valid status code, the new request sequence is
L294@P2: valid and retained (line 33); otherwise, it is discarded and the
L295@P2: received error code is logged for analysis and debugging.
L296@P2: More precisely, the function EXECUTE executes each request in a sequence one by one, each time checking that the
L297@P2: response is valid, extracting and memoizing dynamic objects
L298@P2: (if any), and providing those in subsequent requests in the
L299@P2: sequence if needed, as determined by the dependency analysis;
L300@P2: the response returned by function EXECUTE in line 31 refers
L301@P2: to the response received for the last, newly-appended request
L302@P2: in the sequence. Note that if a request sequence produces
L303@P2: more than one dynamic object of a given type, the function
L304@P2: EXECUTE will memoize all of those objects, but will provide
L305@P2: them later when needed by subsequent requests in the exact
L306@P2: order in which they are produced; in other words, the function
L307@P2: EXECUTE will not try different ordering of such objects. If a
L308@P2: dynamic object is passed as argument to a subsequent request
L309@P2: and is “destroyed” after that request, i.e., it becomes unusable
L310@P2: later on, RESTler will detect this by receiving an invalid status
L311@P2: code (outside the 200 range) when attempting to reuse that
L312@P2: unusable object, and will then discard that request sequence.
L313@P2: By default, the function RENDER of Figure 3 generates all
L314@P2: possible combinations of dictionary values for every request
L315@P2: with several fuzzable types (see line 28). For large dictionaries,
L316@P2: this may result in astronomical numbers of combinations. In
L317@P2: that case, a more scalable option is to randomly sample each
L318@P2: dictionary for one (or a few) values, or to use combinatorialtesting algorithms [10] for covering, say, every dictionary
L319@P2: value, or every pair of values, but not every k-tuple. In the
L320@P2: experiments reported later, we used small dictionaries and the
L321@P2: default RENDER function shown in Figure 3.
L322@P2: The function EXTEND of Figure 3 generates all request sequences of length n+1 whose dependencies are satisfied. Since
L323@P2: n is incremented at each iteration of the main loop of line 8,
L324@P2: the overall algorithm performs a breadth-first search (BFS)
L325@P2: in the search space defined by all possible request sequences.
L326@P2: In Section V, we report experiments performed also with two
L327@P2: additional search strategies: BFS-Fast and RandomWalk.
L328@P2: BFS-Fast. In function EXTEND, instead of appending every
L329@P2: request to every sequence, every request is appended to at most
L330@P2: one sequence. This results in in a smaller set newSeqSet
L331@P2-3: which covers (i.e., includes at least once) every request butdoes not generate all valid request sequences. Like BFS,
L332@P3: BFS-Fast still exercises every executable request type at each
L333@P3: iteration of the main loop in line 8: it still provides full
L334@P3: grammar coverage but with fewer request sequences, which
L335@P3: allows it to go deeper faster than BFS.
L336@P3: RandomWalk. In function EXTEND, the two loops of line 17
L337@P3: and line 18 are eliminated; instead, the function now returns a
L338@P3: single new request sequence whose dependencies are satisfied,
L339@P3: and generated by randomly selecting one request sequence
L340@P3: seq in seqSet and one request in reqSet. (The function
L341@P3: randomly chooses such a pair until all the dependencies of that
L342@P3: pair are satisfied.) This search strategy will therefore explore
L343@P3: the search space of possible request sequences deeper more
L344@P3: quickly than BFS or BFS-Fast. When RandomWalk can no
L345@P3: longer extend the current request sequence, it restarts from
L346@P3: scratch from an empty request sequence. (Since it does not
L347@P3: memoize past request sequences between restarts, it might
L348@P3: regenerate the same request sequence again in the future.)
L349@P3: IV. IMPLEMENTATION
L350@P3: We have implemented RESTler in 3,151 lines of modular
L351@P3: python code split into: the parser and compiler module, the
L352@P3: core fuzzing runtime module, and the garbage collector (GC)
L353@P3: module. The parser and compiler module is used to parse a
L354@P3: Swagger specification and to generate the RESTler grammar
L355@P3: describing how to fuzz a target service. (In the absence of
L356@P3: a Swagger specification, the user could directly provide the
L357@P3: RESTler grammar.) The core fuzzing runtime module implements the algorithm of Figure 3 and its variants. It renders API
L358@P3: requests, processes service-side responses to retrieve values
L359@P3: of the dynamic objects created, and analyzes service-side
L360@P3: feedback to decide which requests should be reused in future
L361@P3: generations while composing new request sequences. Finally,
L362@P3: the GC runs as a separate thread that tracks the creation of
L363@P3: the dynamic objects over time and periodically deletes aging
L364@P3: objects that exceed some user-defined limit (see Section VII).
L365@P3: A. Using RESTler
L366@P3: RESTler is a command-line tool that takes as input a
L367@P3: Swagger specification, service access parameters (e.g. IP,
L368@P3: port, authentication), the mutations dictionary, and the search
L369@P3: strategy to use during fuzzing. After compiling the Swagger
L370@P3: specification, RESTler displays the number of endpoints discovered and the list of resolved and unresolved dependencies,
L371@P3: if any. In case of unresolved dependencies, the user may provide additional annotations or resource-specific mutations (see
L372@P3: Section VII) and re-run this step to resolve them. Alternatively,
L373@P3: the user may choose to start fuzzing right away and RESTler
L374@P3: will treat unresolved dependencies in consumer parameters
L375@P3: as restler_fuzzable string primitives. During fuzzing,
L376@P3: RESTler reports each bug, currently defined as a 500 HTTP
L377@P3: status code (500 “Internal Server Error”) received after executing a request sequence, as soon as it is found.
L378@P3: B. Current Limitations
L379@P3: Currently, RESTler does not support requests for API endpoints with server-side redirects (e.g., 301 “Moved Permanently”, 303 “See Other”, and 307 “Temporary Redirect”).

L911@P8: extensions made to RESTler to address these challenges.
L912@P8: Resource Quotas. Production services that run in public
L913@P8: clouds are deployed with default resource quotas. Once quotas
L914@P8: are reached, RESTler’s core algorithm will continue to try
L915@P8: request sequences containing requests that can no longer
L916@P8: succeed due to exceeded quotas (since these requests were
L917@P8: valid in prior tests and generated lots of new resources), which
L918@P8: impedes progress. This challenge is unique to public cloud
L919@P8: deployments, contrary to self-contained deployments where
L920@P8: one can easily control and reconfigure resource quotas. To
L921@P8: address this problem, we implemented a garbage collector
L922@P8: (GC) in RESTler. The GC runs as a separate thread that
L923@P8: monitors the creation of dynamic resources over time and
L924@P8: periodically deletes dynamic objects that are no longer used in
L925@P8: order to avoid exceeding resource quotas. This allows RESTler
L926@P8: to continuously test new sequences for hours or days without
L971@P8: requests that exercise the business logic exposed by the API
L972@P8-9: in a stateful manner and without pre-recorded HTTP traffic.Feedback-directed Test Generation. The dynamic feedback
L973@P9: RESTler uses to prune invalid requests from the search space
L974@P9: (line 32 in Figure 3) is similar to the feedback used in
L975@P9: Randoop [32]. However, the Randoop search strategy (in
L976@P9: particular, search pruning and ordering) is different from
L977@P9: the three search strategies considered in our work, and the
L978@P9: Randoop optimizations related to object equality and filtering
L979@P9: are not relevant in our context. RESTler’s dependency analysis
L980@P9: is also related to the analysis of type dependencies performed
L981@P9: by the Randoop algorithm [32] for typed object-oriented
L982@P9: programs. However, unlike in the Randoop work, dynamic
L983@P9: objects in Swagger specifications are implicitly declared and
L984@P9: untyped (e.g., authentication tokens or service-specific resources). When a Swagger specification is not complete or
L985@P9: RESTler cannot infer object types correctly, RESTler supports
L986@P9: annotations (see Section VII) that the user can use to fix and
L987@P9: control RESTler’s behavior. In the future, it would be interesting to allow richer user annotations in order to easily specify
L988@P9: complex service-specific types as well as their properties, in
L989@P9: the spirit of code contracts [28], [5].
L990@P9: Model-based Testing. Our BFS-Fast search strategy is inspired by test generation algorithms used in model-based
L991@P9: testing [42], whose goal is to generate a minimum number of
L992@P9: tests covering, say, every state and transition of a finite-state
L993@P9: machine model (e.g., see [43]) in order to generate a test suite
L994@P9: to check conformance of a (blackbox) implementation with
L995@P9: respect to that model. BFS-Fast is also related to algorithms
L996@P9: for generating tests from an input grammar while covering all
L997@P9: its production rules [26]. Indeed, in our context, BFS-Fast provides, by construction, a full grammar coverage up to the given
L998@P9: current sequence length. The number of request sequences
L999@P9: it generates is not necessarily minimal, but that number was
L1000@P9: always small, hence manageable, in our experiments so far.
L1001@P9: Grammar-based Fuzzing. General-purpose grammar-based
L1002@P9: fuzzers like Peach [33] and SPIKE [37], among others [39], are
L1003@P9: not Swagger-specific but can also be used to fuzz REST APIs.
L1004@P9: With these tools, however, the user has to manually construct
L1005@P9: an API-specific input grammar, often encoded directly by code
L1006@P9: specifying what and how to fuzz, similar to the code shown
L1007@P9: on the right of Figure 2. By contrast, RESTler automatically
L1008@P9: generates an input grammar from a Swagger specification, and
L1009@P9: its fuzzing rules are determined separately and automatically
L1010@P9: by the algorithm of Figure 3.
L1011@P9: Automatically learning input grammars from input samples is another complementary research area [25], [6], [24],
L1012@P9: [36]. RESTler currently relies on a Swagger specification to
L1013@P9: represent a service’s input space and it learns automatically
L1014@P9: how to prune invalid request sequences by analyzing service
L1015@P9: responses. Still, a Swagger specification could be further
L1016@P9: refined given representative unit tests or live traffic in order
L1017@P9: to focus the search towards specific areas of the input space.
L1018@P9: For REST services without a Swagger specification, it would
L1019@P9: be worth investigating how to automatically infer it by using
L1020@P9: machine learning on runtime traffic logs or static analysis on
L1021@P9: the code implementing the API.
L1022@P9: Whitebox Fuzzing. Grammar-based fuzzing can also be combined [27], [21] with whitebox fuzzing [23], which uses
L1023@P9: dynamic symbolic execution [22], [9], constraint generation
L1024@P9: and solving in order to generate new tests exercising new
L1025@P9: code paths. In contrast, RESTler is currently purely blackbox:
L1026@P9: the inner workings of the service under test are invisible to
L1027@P9: RESTler which only sees REST API requests and responses.
L1028@P9: Since cloud services are usually complex distributed systems
L1029@P9: whose components are written in different languages, general
L1030@P9: symbolic-execution-based approaches seem problematic, but
L1031@P9: it would be worth exploring this option further. For instance,
L1032@P9: in the short term, RESTler could be extended to take into
L1033@P9: account alerts (e.g., assertion violations) reported in back-end
L1034@P9: logs in order to increase chances of finding interesting bugs
L1035@P9: and correlating them to specific request sequences.

L743@P6: First, we compare BFS with BFS-fast. We observe that after
L744@P6: five hours, BFS achieves better coverage than BFS-Fast in

L748@P6: not scale well in APIs with relatively more requests, such as
L749@P6: Issues, Groups, and Projects. As shown in Table II after 5

L765@P6: BFS-Fast. RandomWalk also delivers the best coverage after
